          Late Goals, Struggles Versus 10 Men, Unable to Hold a Lead: Do Man Utd Have a Mentality Problem?
        
      
                          
                      Oct 13, 2026
          
                      Ryan Benson / Author, Yash Thakur / Data Viz
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
Manchester United once again failed to make the most of their opposition having a man sent off on Saturday, but that's not the only reason some critics might question their mentality.

It hadn’t been pretty, but Manchester United were practically there; just their second win of the Premier League season was within touching distance as they entered the final 10 minutes of regulation time against Tottenham 1-0 up and with a man advantage at Old Trafford.

Rodrigo Bentancur nudging his forehead into Luke Shaw’s face in response to the United full-back shoving him to the floor yielded a red card for the Uruguayan with 78 minutes on the clock. It capped a bad few moments for Spurs, who’d gone behind to Bryan Mbeumo’s well-placed finished just five minutes earlier.

Bentancur’s dismissal was, obviously, greeted with jubilation among the majority of those at Old Trafford. For Michael Carrick on the touchline, thoughts must have turned to how his team were going to react to the situation.

He won’t have needed any reminding about what occurred the last time United played against a team with 10 men, when they seemed to wilt under the added expectation that accompanied Phil Foden’s red card in last month’s 1-0 Manchester derby defeat, highly controversial though Manchester City's win was.
At least on this occasion United already had the lead and only needed to hold on for 12 minutes plus added time.

Of course, they didn’t manage to. Sandro Tonali’s cross in the second minute of stoppage time was glanced in by Dominic Solanke during his intimate embrace/wrestling bout with Lisandro Martínez, and Tottenham – deservedly, it should be emphasised – equalised to ultimately earn a 1-1 draw.

Tottenham were comfortably the better team over the course of the 90 minutes, to the point where even a win for United wouldn’t have earned them or Carrick that much credit. Spurs went into the game bottom of the table but played their hosts off the park at times, especially during the first 30 minutes.
The outcome produced two especially damning facts for United.

Firstly, it was the third successive occasion on which they’d failed to beat a team who started the day bottom of the table, having also drawn 1-1 with Fulham prior to the international break and with Wolves in December 2025.

Then, it was also the third time in a row that they’d failed to defeat opposition who’d been reduced to 10 men, the other occasions being at home to City last month (1-0 loss) and at Newcastle in March (2-1 loss).

Considering those facts, it’s perfectly understandable that United’s mentality might be called into question. All are instances where they would be favourites to win, even accounting for City being a very, very good team who benefited from a goal that shouldn't have stood.
Aside from the aforementioned controversy surrounding Erling Haaland's goal, there aren’t really any redeeming factors from the six games noted.

In December’s 1-1 draw with rock-bottom Wolves at Old Trafford, United were desperately poor, generating just 0.84 xG to their visitors’ 1.16. And this was a Wolves side who finished 2025 with the worst points-per-game ratio (0.76) over a full year of Premier League football since 2018 (Huddersfield Town – 0.62).

In the loss to 10-man Newcastle, the Red Devils had the whole second half with an extra man. But even then, the two best chances of the second period fell to Newcastle, and neither of them even resulted in a goal.
And the draw with Fulham last month; sure, United were unfortunate to trail to Martínez’s own goal, but they were also very lucky to earn a point via Matheus Cunha’s late deflected shot.

Many United fans will also remember November’s dismal 1-0 home defeat to Everton, when the visitors had Idrissa Gueye sent off in the 13th minute for tussling with his own teammate. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall netted 16 minutes later and that proved decisive.
It could all be a massive coincidence. After all, there have been other occasions since the start of last season when United have overcome 10-man opposition or other teams they’d be expected to beat.
But situations like Saturday have become all too familiar; and it is increasingly difficult to argue it’s just a coincidence.
Since the start of last season in all competitions, United have played seven matches in which their opponents have been reduced to 10 men; they’ve won just three of them, losing as many.
